Every actual duration is still NEEDS-DECISION or LEGAL-REVIEW, the named reviewers are not appointed, and the approver of role deletion is not recorded.
items.security_impact: MEDIUM for Phase 2. It becomes HIGH at first tenant offboarding: without a retention rule, tenant roles and tenant data are either destroyed too early (losing audit evidence) or kept indefinitely (a privacy exposure).

items.title: Disposition of a reserved entitlement after its original period ends
items.why_unresolved: When a student is archived inside the reversal window the credit is returned; when archived outside it, the entitlement is held as reserved. What happens to that reserved entitlement once its original period has elapsed — expire, extend, return, or convert — is a commercial rule that has not been decided.
items.security_impact: LOW for security, HIGH for billing correctness. A wrong rule silently gives away or silently destroys paid credit.
items.continue_conditions: Reactivation against a reserved entitlement is implemented and tested; no expiry, extension or automatic return of a reserved entitlement is implemented. Nothing reads the elapsed period.
options: A. The reserved entitlement expires at the end of its original period and the credit is not returned.
B. The reserved entitlement expires but the credit is returned to the wallet.
C. The reserved entitlement is held indefinitely until it is reused or explicitly released.
D. The period is extended by the archived duration, so the counselor loses no paid time.
items.rationale: It matches what the counselor paid for (a quantity of service, not a wall-clock window), it cannot destroy paid credit, and unlike C it is bounded. This is a recommendation for the Product Owner, not a decision: nothing in the implementation assumes it.
items.code_resolution_note: Nothing expires or returns a reserved entitlement; the rule itself is undecided.
items.closure_evidence: A Product Owner rule for post-period disposition, then implementation and CRD tests for each outcome.

items.title: Canonical wire format and signing for Saga envelopes
items.why_unresolved: The outbox envelope carries payload_hash, schema_version and correlation identifiers, but the canonical byte encoding, the hash and signature algorithms, and the key policy are not decided. They depend on PS-1..PS-4.
items.security_impact: HIGH. Without authenticated transport, a Workspace cannot distinguish a genuine ownership-switch event from a forged one, which is a cross-tenant takeover path.
items.continue_conditions: apply_inbox_event() is fail-closed through assert_inbox_transport_verified(). The working projection exists only as apply_inbox_event_synthetic() under the synthetic inbox role (D-014). No signature is invented and no authenticity is claimed.
options: A. Decide PS-1..PS-4 first and derive this from them.
B. Define the canonical encoding now (which is a deterministic serialization question) and leave the algorithms to PS-1/PS-2.
C. Keep the whole item closed until Phase 18/19.
items.rationale: Canonical encoding is independent of the cipher choice and is the part that silently breaks compatibility if decided late; it can be settled without pre-empting Platform Security.
items.code_resolution_note: Implementable once the wire format and signature scheme are chosen; until then envelopes are rejected.
items.closure_evidence: Approved canonical format and signature scheme, published test vectors, and verifier tests that reject every malformed or mis-signed envelope.

items.title: Resolution of a quarantined inbox event
items.why_unresolved: An inbox event that fails verification or integrity is quarantined. Who may inspect it, who may release or discard it, and what evidence that requires is not decided.
items.security_impact: HIGH. A release path is an authenticated-transport bypass if its authority is not defined; without any path, a single bad event can strand a student's ownership.
items.continue_conditions: Quarantine records the outcome and stops the projection. No release or discard command exists. Forward recovery is operator re-drive of the delivery at the Control Plane, which never alters the event.
options: A. No release path: a quarantined event is always re-issued as a new event by the Control Plane.
B. A two-person operator release with recorded evidence.
C. Platform-admin release with audit.
items.rationale: It keeps the immutable-event guarantee intact and needs no new authority: re-drive and re-issue already exist. B and C both create a privileged path that would have to be defended against misuse.
items.code_resolution_note: A quarantined event stays quarantined; who may release it, and how, is undecided.
items.closure_evidence: A decided release authority and procedure, then tests that only that authority can release and that release is audited.

items.title: Item-bank ownership and the meaning of item_ref
items.why_unresolved: Assessment version questions reference items by item_ref, but whether the item bank is platform-owned, Workspace-owned or external, and therefore what referential integrity is enforceable, is not decided.
items.security_impact: MEDIUM. A Workspace-owned bank referenced without integrity is an unrestricted polymorphic reference, which the brief forbids; a platform-owned bank crosses the tenant boundary and needs its own authorization rule.
items.continue_conditions: item_ref is a constrained text reference inside the Workspace with no cross-database FK and no claim of integrity against an external bank. The immutable question set itself is implemented and tested.
options: A. Workspace-owned item bank with a real foreign key.
B. Platform-owned shared bank with explicit licensing and read authorization.
C. Both, distinguished by a reference kind, with integrity enforced per kind.
items.rationale: It is the only option that gives enforceable referential integrity inside Phase 2's tenancy model, and C can be added later without rewriting A.
items.code_resolution_note: Item-bank ownership is a content/licensing decision.
items.closure_evidence: Decided ownership and item_ref semantics, then schema constraints and ASM tests.

items.title: Which scoring algorithms are permitted, and how are their versions governed
items.why_unresolved: Batch 4 made the scoring algorithm and its version explicit in every scoring policy snapshot, because nothing recorded which algorithm produced a score — a snapshot of `{}` was accepted and published. The database now requires the snapshot to NAME an algorithm and a positive integer version. It deliberately does not constrain WHICH algorithm names are permitted, who may introduce one, or what a version increment means, because those are product decisions about scoring behaviour.
items.security_impact: LOW for security, MEDIUM for correctness and auditability. Without a governed set, two Workspaces could use the same algorithm name for different behaviour, and a historical score would no longer be attributable to a known rule.
items.continue_conditions: The database stores and compares snapshots and never computes or validates a score. The shape is enforced (EXM-01..07, EXM-42); the value set is not. No algorithm is implemented anywhere.
options: A. A platform-level registry of algorithm names and versions, referenced by the snapshot.
B. A fixed allowlist in the schema, extended only by migration.
C. Free-form names, with governance left to process rather than the database.
items.rationale: A registry makes a historical score attributable to a named, versioned rule without freezing the set in the schema, and it is the only option under which a reviewer can tell what `algorithm_version: 2` meant at the time. Not decided; nothing in the implementation assumes it.
items.code_resolution_note: Which scoring algorithms are allowed is a pedagogical decision; the schema already refuses unversioned scoring.
items.closure_evidence: An approved algorithm list with versioning rules, then tests that refuse anything else.

Its canonical hierarchy is Grade -> Subject -> Book/Edition -> Chapter -> Topic -> Subtopic, and its own section 7 leaves open whether books/editions are MVP-managed or imported from a controlled source, whether a Workspace may fork reference nodes or only overlay them, who approves curriculum changes, and whether subtopic-level mastery is mandatory in MVP. Neither property can be tested while the ownership structures are absent.

Every foreign key restricts deletion, so no curriculum node can be deleted out from under the history that references it (CUR-09 asserts this from the catalog). Mastery stays at topic level.

options: A. Approve the curriculum contract and build Book/Edition, successor mapping and ownership metadata in Phase 7 (Curriculum), where the roadmap already places it.
B. Build Book/Edition now in Phase 2 to complete the hierarchy, deferring only mastery and licensing.

Building Book/Edition now (B) would commit to an import model and an ownership model that have not been chosen, and those choices are hard to reverse once curriculum rows reference them.

items.title: Normalized PlanItem model versus today's opaque plan_content JSON
items.why_unresolved: DETERMINISTIC_PLANNING_DOMAIN_CONTRACT.md is marked DRAFT / NOT APPROVED. Its section 1 states that planning inputs and outputs 'must be modeled as first-class domain data, not hidden inside an opaque JSON blob', and section 4 specifies a normalized PlanItem with typed nullable foreign keys and exactly-one-source constraints. Today student_plan_versions carries plan_content as jsonb, which is exactly the shape the contract rejects. The Product Owner scoped the 2026-11-15 work to exclude it.
items.security_impact: LOW for security. HIGH for the product's core promise: with the plan in a blob there is no referential integrity from a plan item to the topic, activity, exam or review it schedules; no per-item status; no machine-readable deferral reason; and no way to answer 'what was originally planned, what changed and why' by query, which PROJECT_MASTER_PROMPT sections 31, 72 and 81 require.
items.continue_conditions: Plan and PlanVersion identity, versioning, immutability of a published version and version history all exist and are tested. plan_content is stored but nothing in the database interprets it, so no scheduling behaviour is implied or claimed. student_plan_versions is now covered by the transfer write barrier through its plan (FRZ-01c, FRZ-18b).
options: A. Build normalized plan_items in Phase 12 (Planning Engine), where the roadmap places the engine that produces them.
B. Build the plan_items data model now in Phase 2 — typed FKs and exactly-one-source constraints, no scheduling logic — so the engine later has a schema to write into.
C. Keep plan_content as the authority and accept that plan contents have no referential integrity.
items.rationale: The data model is a Phase 2 concern and the engine is not: the same split already worked for Activity, whose typed source columns and exactly-one-source CHECK were built in Phase 2 while nothing generates activities yet. Deciding the shape later is what makes it expensive, because by then plan_content blobs exist and have to be migrated. (C) is the only option that conflicts with the contract outright. This is a recommendation; nothing is built against it.
items.code_resolution_note: A normalized PlanItem model is schema work once chosen; today plan_content is opaque JSON, so planning constraints cannot be enforced by the database.
items.closure_evidence: A decided PlanItem model, then schema, constraints and tests for the planning invariants (no conflicts, no impossible workload, no duplicates).

items.title: Counselor-to-counselor isolation inside one Workspace
items.why_unresolved: The Supervisor brief requires that no counselor may access another counselor's students, even within the same Organization. The database does not enforce this and cannot today: measured on 2026-11-15, there is NO row-level security on any table in the Workspace database, and the Workspace runtime role holds SELECT on 47 tables in full. Tenant isolation in this design is per-Workspace — one database per Workspace with no cross-database grants, which the cross-database denial step does test — so every counselor inside a Workspace shares one runtime identity. Whether the boundary is enforced by row-level security keyed to the counselor assignment, by a per-counselor database role, or only in an application layer is an architecture decision that has not been made. UPDATE 2026-11-18: the boundary is now implemented in workspace_counselor_scope_draft.sql (counselor_may_access_student, counselor_visible_students, counselor_may_access_row, counselor_caseload_report) and tested by ISO-C1..ISO-54 against guessed ids, list queries, a report, related records in all 32 student-scoped tables, note visibility and revocation; two write paths are enforced (counselor notes; the notification recipient rule, which Batch 8 had left open to any active member). What remains is binding the caller: every boundary function takes the membership as an argument and the database cannot verify it, so enforcement is not possible without a Platform Security decision on the principal mechanism.
items.security_impact: CRITICAL as a design finding, and BLOCKING for the Phase 2 gate. It is a core product security requirement (master prompt section 3; API authorization contract sections 4 and 6; role-grantability matrix), and the database currently fails OPEN on it: the single runtime role every counselor shares reads all 32 student-scoped tables in full, including other counselors' private notes (ISO-GAP-01..03, measured). Exposure today is nil only because no API or deployment exists; the first code path built on this schema would inherit cross-counselor access by default. The boundary half is now implemented (2026-11-18); the caller-binding half is not.
items.continue_conditions: Other implementation may continue; the Phase 2 gate may not pass. SEC-10 and ISO-GAP-01..03 assert the residual as OPEN lines that fail the suite if the measurement changes, so the record cannot go stale silently. No document claims counselor-to-counselor isolation is enforced.
items.decision_owner: Platform Security (caller binding) with the Product Owner and the architecture owner
options: A. Per-membership database login roles mapped to memberships by a reviewed table; row-level security reads session_user. Identity is verified by PostgreSQL itself; cost is one role per staff member and constraints on connection pooling.

B. A short-lived signed principal assertion verified inside the database by a SECURITY DEFINER function (the receipt-verifier pattern this project already has), which records the verified membership for the current transaction only; row-level security reads that. Works with pooling; depends on PS-1..PS-4.
C. Enforce in the API only, keeping the database boundary functions as defence in depth. Weakest: any other code path with the runtime role bypasses it, which is exactly today's state.
D. One Workspace per counselor. Removes the problem by construction but contradicts the Organization model the product requires.
items.recommended_option: B, with A as the fallback if PS-1..PS-4 cannot be decided in time
items.rationale: B binds the caller cryptographically without one database role per person and reuses infrastructure already designed and tested here (Ed25519 receipt verification, fail-closed verifier). A is simpler and PostgreSQL-native and is the right fallback. C leaves the database failing open, which is the finding. D contradicts the approved Organization model. Session GUCs are not an option: H-03 already rejected them as an authorization mechanism, because the application sets them and so can forge them.
items.code_resolution_note: The BOUNDARY (who may reach which student) is implemented and tested as of 2026-11-18. Binding the CALLER to a membership needs a Platform Security decision; after it, enforcement (row-level security over the 32 student-scoped tables) is implementation work. This is the only item whose current state fails OPEN rather than closed.
items.closure_evidence: A decided caller-binding mechanism; row-level security on every student-scoped table keyed to counselor_may_access_student; ISO-GAP-01..03 turned from OPEN into failing-if-reachable assertions; cross-counselor negative tests run AS each counselor's own identity rather than as the shared runtime role; independent review.

items.title: Control Plane topology and recovery — numeric objectives
items.why_unresolved: Option A is accepted: independent Control Plane infrastructure, primary plus replica, independently controlled encrypted backups with restore drills, fail-closed student access when ownership cannot be validated. RPO, RTO, retention, failover consistency, split-brain prevention and measured capacity/cost remain open.
items.security_impact: HIGH at operation, not at schema. Without a split-brain rule, two Control Plane primaries could both grant ownership.
items.continue_conditions: Phase 2 produces schema and commands only. No deployment, no replication configuration and no availability claim. The fail-closed ownership rule is implemented.
items.decision_owner: Product Owner with the operations owner
options: A. Set RPO/RTO now from business tolerance and design to them.
B. Measure a representative workload first, then set them.
C. Defer to Phase 28 (Production Readiness).
items.rationale: The brief forbids inventing SLOs, and numbers set without measurement would be either unachievable or meaningless. Measurement needs a running system, so this belongs with Phase 27/28 work, but the split-brain prevention rule should be decided earlier because it constrains the design.
items.code_resolution_note: Numeric RPO/RTO and topology are operational decisions; nothing in Phase 2 deploys anything.
items.closure_evidence: Decided objectives, then an operations phase with measured restore and failover drills.

items.title: Transfer cutover — freeze boundary, duration, recovery and acceptance thresholds
items.why_unresolved: Option B is accepted: controlled source write freeze, final snapshot, destination staging and import, integrity validation, then the atomic Control Plane ownership switch. The freeze duration, the precise freeze boundary, failure recovery and acceptance thresholds were explicitly left to detailed design and tests.
items.security_impact: HIGH. An imprecise freeze boundary means writes accepted after the snapshot are lost or applied to the wrong owner.
items.continue_conditions: The database half of the freeze boundary is now implemented and tested (see docs/phase2/workspace/workspace_transfer_freeze.sql): a durable freeze record, a write barrier on every student-scoped table, an in-flight transaction barrier with a recorded watermark, and a permanent fence after the switch. No freeze duration, drain timeout or acceptance threshold is invented or enforced. The application, worker, import and export surfaces named in the contract do not exist in this repository and are not claimed.
items.decision_owner: Product Owner with the operations owner
options: A. Set a maximum freeze duration and an acceptance threshold now, as a product promise.
B. Derive both from measured transfer runs once a service layer exists.
C. Leave the freeze open-ended and require manual operator confirmation per transfer.
items.rationale: A duration invented without a measured workload is the kind of number the brief forbids. C is acceptable as an interim operating rule while B is being measured, and the database already supports it because the freeze has no timeout.
items.code_resolution_note: The database half of the freeze is implemented and tested; the controller, its timeouts and acceptance thresholds need decisions and a service that does not exist.
items.closure_evidence: Decided thresholds, a controller implementation, and end-to-end cutover tests including timeout and recovery.

items.title: Signature algorithm for authorization assertions
items.why_unresolved: Deferred to Platform Security (Issue #13, Decision C). No algorithm has been chosen.
items.security_impact: HIGH. Blocks production verification of every assertion and receipt.
items.continue_conditions: The production verifier is fail-closed. Tests use test doubles only and are labelled as such.
options: B. ECDSA P-256.
C. RSA-PSS.
D. HMAC with a shared key.

items.title: Algorithm allowlist values
items.why_unresolved: Depends on PS-1 and has not been decided.

items.title: Key provisioning, storage, rotation and revocation procedures
items.why_unresolved: Deferred to Platform Security. No procedure exists.
items.security_impact: HIGH. Rotation without a procedure is an outage; compromise without revocation is unbounded.
items.continue_conditions: Contact-identity HMAC rotation is implemented as a mechanism only. No key policy, rotation schedule or revocation source is invented.
options: A. KMS-managed rotation with overlapping validity.
B. Manual rotation under a runbook.
C. No rotation before the pilot.
items.rationale: Overlapping validity is what makes rotation possible without downtime, and it has to be designed before the first key is issued.
items.code_resolution_note: Key provisioning, storage, rotation and revocation are operational procedures.
items.closure_evidence: Documented procedures and a rotation drill.

items.title: Clock-skew allowance for not_before / expires_at
items.why_unresolved: Deferred; no allowance has been set.
items.security_impact: MEDIUM. Too large an allowance extends the life of a revoked assertion; too small causes spurious failures.
items.continue_conditions: No skew allowance is implemented. Expiry comparisons use clock_timestamp() with no tolerance.
options: A. Zero tolerance plus mandatory NTP.
B. A small fixed allowance (for example 30 seconds).
C. A configurable allowance with an upper bound.
items.rationale: A bounded configurable value survives real deployment conditions without being an unbounded weakening.
items.code_resolution_note: A clock-skew allowance is a policy value.
items.closure_evidence: A decided value and boundary tests at exactly the allowance.

items.title: Revocation source for receipts and propagation of membership revocation
items.why_unresolved: Deferred. No revocation source is defined for API, export, worker or notification handoffs.
items.security_impact: HIGH. Blocks any end-to-end freshness claim: a revoked membership may still be honoured downstream.
items.continue_conditions: No freshness or end-to-end revocation claim is made anywhere in Phase 2. Governance events record revocation in the database; propagation beyond it is not implemented.
options: A. Short-lived receipts, no revocation list.
B. A revocation list consulted on every use.
C. Both: short lifetimes plus a list for emergencies.

items.title: Membership role source of truth and trusted authorization
items.why_unresolved: The competing-role-source part is closed: the scalar workspace_memberships.role_key is gone and membership_roles is the canonical projection. What remains open is the trusted authorization adapter: authenticated actor evidence is not cryptographically verified, no grantability/anti-self-escalation matrix is enforced, and no application role may execute the governance commands. That depends on Issue #13 and PS-1..PS-8.
items.security_impact: HIGH. Until it is closed, a governance command has no verifiable authority behind it, so role grants cannot be trusted as an authorization basis.
items.continue_conditions: Governance commands are restricted to dedicated owner roles; no application role can append events; the production verifier is fail-closed; verifier_rt was tested to hold no receipt-consumption or governance privilege.
options: A1/B3 as proposed in Issue #13: a trusted governance authorization adapter with a fail-closed verifier.
B. A database-only authority model with no external verification.
C. Defer governance commands entirely out of Phase 2.
items.rationale: It is the option already proposed and reviewed in Issue #13, and it is the only one that lets a role grant carry evidence of who authorized it. B would make the database its own authority, which is what the current fail-closed design deliberately avoids.
items.code_resolution_note: The competing role source is closed; the trusted authorization adapter is implementable once Issue #13 and PS-1..PS-8 are decided. Governance commands are uncallable by application roles meanwhile.
items.closure_evidence: A verified authorization adapter, an enforced grantability/anti-self-escalation matrix, and tests that a forged or self-granted role is refused.

items.title: Who may authorize a transfer approval-conflict exception
items.why_unresolved: Separation of duties means the same actor may not both request and approve a transfer. Whether an exception may ever be granted, by whom, with what evidence, and with what audit, is not decided.
items.security_impact: HIGH. An exception path is a separation-of-duties bypass, which is the control that prevents a single actor from moving a student between Workspaces unilaterally.
items.continue_conditions: transfer_approval_conflict_exceptions exists with CHECK (enabled = false), so no exception can be enabled by any role. The table exists only so that the decision has somewhere to land; it grants nothing today.
options: A. No exception ever: a conflict must be resolved by involving a second actor.
B. Platform-admin exception with recorded justification and audit.
C. Two-person platform-admin exception.
items.rationale: The control exists precisely for the single-actor case, and an exception path reintroduces exactly the risk it was built to prevent. If an exception is required for operational reasons, C is preferable to B because it does not rely on one administrator's judgement.
items.code_resolution_note: Who may authorize an exception is a governance decision; exceptions are refused meanwhile.
items.closure_evidence: A decided authority, then tests that only it can authorize and that every exception is audited.

items.title: Disposition of pull requests #8, #9, #10 and #11
items.why_unresolved: All four are open drafts against main at ba5e9d8 (verified 2026-11-14 by reading the repository). PR #12 does not merge or supersede their Git history. Whether each is to be merged, closed as superseded, or rebased has not been instructed.
items.security_impact: NONE directly. The risk is process: four open drafts of the same documentation make it ambiguous which text is current.
items.continue_conditions: No PR is merged, rebased, force-pushed or closed by the implementation. Work continues only on the PR #12 branch.
options: A. Close #8-#11 as superseded by #12, after confirming no unique content is lost.
B. Merge them in order, then rebase #12.
C. Leave all five open until Phase 2 is approved.
items.rationale: Their content has been consolidated into the #12 branch, and keeping four stale drafts open invites a reviewer to read superseded text. The confirmation that no unique content is lost should be produced before closing; the implementation can prepare that diff on request.
items.code_resolution_note: A process decision about four open pull requests.
items.closure_evidence: A Product Owner instruction per PR (merge, close as superseded, or rebase) and its execution by the Product Owner.

items.title: Branch synchronization: the PR #12 branch is behind main by two commits whose net content change is zero
items.why_unresolved: The PR #12 branch IS behind main. This entry previously claimed the opposite and that claim was WRONG. The error: main's tip was read from the `base.sha` field of the open pull request objects, which records the base commit as it stood when each PR was created (ba5e9d8), not main's current tip. Measured correctly on 2026-11-15: main is at 5bb8e4ed07a7c770ecba7c506a1d2c278e36b6d6 and `git merge-base --is-ancestor 5bb8e4e HEAD` fails, so the branch does not contain main. Substantively, however, nothing from main is missing: main's two extra commits are 4004360, which added docs/phase2/control_plane/tests/cp_30_role_privilege_tests.sql, and 5bb8e4e, which reverted it. `git diff ba5e9d8 5bb8e4e` reports ZERO changed files, so merging main would bring no file changes. The branch's own cp_30_role_privilege_tests.sql was written independently on this branch and is unaffected.
items.security_impact: NONE technically. The real risk is to the integrity of this project's own reporting: a false 'corrected' claim sat in the register and in PROJECT_STATE.md for several batches, and a reviewer relying on it would have believed the branch was synchronized when it was not.
items.continue_conditions: No rebase, no merge and no force-push, per the standing constraint. The divergence is two commits with zero net content difference, so no work on this branch depends on resolving it.
options: A. Leave the branch as it is. It is behind main only in history, and main carries no content the branch lacks.
B. Merge main into the branch so the history is strictly ahead, once the Product Owner lifts the no-merge constraint for this one operation.
C. Resolve it together with the PR #8-#11 disposition, since merging or closing those will move main anyway.
items.rationale: The divergence is harmless today (zero net content), so there is nothing to gain from a merge on its own, and rebasing or force-pushing is forbidden. Dispositioning PR #8-#11 will move main regardless, so the synchronization decision belongs with that one rather than being taken twice. Whichever is chosen, the claim in the record must now say 'behind by two commits, zero net content difference' rather than 'not behind'.

commits_on_main_not_on_branch: 4004360 test(phase2): verify claim admission executor is isolated
5bb8e4e revert: remove accidental malformed Phase 2 test from main
evidence.previous_claim: FACTUALLY_CORRECTED / not behind main — this was wrong and is retracted

items.code_resolution_note: Two commits with zero net content; a merge of main into the branch would resolve it, but merging is not authorized.
items.closure_evidence: An authorized merge (or the PR #8-#11 disposition moving main) and a re-verification that the branch contains main.

items.title: Who may place and who may release a legal hold
items.why_unresolved: The data-retention contract section 9 lists 'Legal hold categories, triggers, release authority and dispute handling' as still required, and section 5 adds that 'a hold cannot be released by the same unrestricted deletion job that it blocks'. Neither the category list nor the two authorities have been decided. Batch 8 built the hold mechanism — resolvable target, immutable placement, one-way release, no delete, no truncate — but deciding WHO places and WHO releases a hold is a Product Owner decision with legal input, and inventing it would be exactly the kind of implicit decision the brief forbids.
items.security_impact: HIGH at pilot. A hold that the wrong party can place is a denial-of-service on lawful deletion; a hold that the wrong party can release is the removal of a legal control. Today neither is possible because no application role can write the table at all, so the exposure is zero while the decision is open and becomes HIGH the moment a role is granted.
items.continue_conditions: No role is granted INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on legal_holds; only the NOLOGIN table owner can write it, which is a synthetic posture and is stated as such in workspace_roles_setup_draft.sql. OPS-51 asserts that from the catalog and fails if any application role is granted a write. The placement and release mechanics are enforced and tested (OPS-30..OPS-36) independently of who is eventually authorized.
items.decision_owner: Product Owner with qualified Iranian legal review
options: A. Platform Admin places and releases holds, with the request recorded against a case reference and a second Platform Admin approving the release.
B. A dedicated compliance role, separate from both the Workspace counselor roles and the deletion executor, holds both capabilities.
C. The Workspace owner may place a hold on their own Workspace's data, while release requires Platform Admin.
D. Holds are placed only through an operational runbook outside the application, by the database owner.
items.rationale: The contract's own rule is that the releasing authority must be separable from the deletion job, which is a separation-of-duties requirement, and this project already has the pattern for it in the transfer approval separation. A dedicated compliance role makes that separation a grant rather than a convention. (A) is workable but conflates platform administration with legal custody. (C) lets the party with an interest in deleting data also place and lift the control over it. (D) leaves no audit trail inside the system, which contradicts the contract's requirement to preserve who placed and released a hold, when, with what authority reference.

evidence.grants: no application role holds INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on legal_holds (asserted, not assumed)

items.code_resolution_note: Who places and releases a hold is a legal-authority decision; nobody can write the table meanwhile.
items.closure_evidence: A decided authority, a grant to exactly that role, and tests that every other role is refused.

items.title: Who authorizes and who executes an irreversible disposition
items.why_unresolved: The retention contract section 4 step 5 requires independent approval for irreversible actions 'according to the approved authority matrix', and states that 'the requester cannot approve their own high-impact deletion'. That matrix does not exist, and no disposition executor identity exists in this repository — there is no job runner, no object-store client and no worker. Batch 8 built the fail-closed gate every future executor must pass; it did not invent the authority that would call it.
items.security_impact: HIGH at pilot. An unauthorized or self-approved deletion is irreversible and may destroy records that a legal or tax obligation requires. Today the exposure is zero: the gate is executable by nobody, and there is no code path that deletes a student, a file object, a notification or an audit event.
items.continue_conditions: EXECUTE on assert_destructive_disposition_allowed() is revoked from PUBLIC and granted to no role; OPS-50 asserts that from the catalog. The gate refuses every destructive action anyway while no retention policy version is approved (Q-020). No deletion path exists for the registered entity types: the file, notification and hold guards refuse DELETE outright, and the audit log refuses UPDATE, DELETE and now TRUNCATE.
items.decision_owner: Product Owner with the operations owner
options: A. Two-party authorization: a compliance role requests, a Platform Admin approves, and a dedicated executor identity — distinct from both — performs the work and may do nothing else.
B. Single approver with full audit, relying on the append-only disposition audit trail for accountability.
C. No automated destructive disposition at all in the first production release: restrict access and archive only, with erasure performed by a reviewed manual runbook.
D. Let the Workspace owner authorize disposition of their own Workspace's data.
items.rationale: (C) first, because an executor that cannot yet verify completeness across object storage, exports, caches, indexes, replicas and backups (OPS-RETENTION-SCOPE) would report deletions it did not actually complete, which is worse than not deleting. Then (A), because it satisfies the contract's requester-is-not-approver rule as a grant and keeps the executor's privileges narrow enough to be reviewable. (B) relies on detection after the fact for an irreversible action. (D) puts the decision with the party most likely to want the data gone and least likely to know the legal obligations.

evidence.measured: the gate refuses for five distinct named reasons and ALLOWS only with a synthetic approved policy inserted inside the test, which is how its refusals are shown to be decisions rather than an unconditional raise

items.code_resolution_note: Who authorizes and executes disposition is undecided; the gate is uncallable meanwhile.
items.closure_evidence: A decided authority matrix with requester != approver, an executor identity, and tests that self-approval is refused.

items.title: Disposition completeness beyond the primary row: objects, exports, caches, indexes, replicas and backups
items.why_unresolved: The retention contract is explicit that 'deletion from the primary row alone is not complete disposition' (section 2) and that restore must re-apply post-backup suppression before recovered data is served (section 7). None of those systems exists in this repository: there is no object store, no export pipeline, no cache, no search index, no replica and no backup tooling. The mechanics also depend on the hosting target, which is itself undecided (OQ-D).
items.security_impact: HIGH at pilot, but as an incompleteness rather than a hole: a deletion reported as done while copies survive is a false compliance statement. Today nothing deletes anything, so no such statement can be made by the system.
items.continue_conditions: Batch 8 claims the database half ONLY, and says so in workspace_operations_draft.sql, in the test header and in PHASE2_EXIT_CRITERIA.md: no completeness of erasure is claimed, retention contract section 7 is recorded as unimplemented, and the gate's own documentation states that passing it is not evidence that a deletion would be complete.
items.decision_owner: Product Owner with the operations owner, after the hosting decision (OQ-D)
options: A. Build a durable suppression ledger that every restore and every derived copy must consult before serving data, and make disposition verification read it.
B. Cryptographic erasure per student or per category, accepting the key-scope, shared-object and backup dependencies the contract requires to be proven first.
C. Bounded backup rotation only, disclosing residual copies until expiry and refusing to report a deletion as complete until rotation has passed.
D. Defer all of it to a later phase and state in the product documentation that erasure is partial until then.
items.rationale: A suppression ledger is the only option that survives a restore, which is the case the contract names explicitly and the one most likely to resurrect deleted data silently. (C) is complementary and honest about residuals rather than overstating them. (B) is attractive but the contract itself requires key scope, shared-object dependencies, backups, holds and recovery behaviour to be proven before cryptographic erasure may be relied on, and none of that can be proven here. (D) alone leaves a compliance statement no one can support.

evidence.not_implemented: no object store, export, cache, index, replica or backup tooling exists in this repository

items.code_resolution_note: A suppression ledger and completeness verification are implementable once the hosting target is decided; none of the systems involved exists yet.
items.closure_evidence: An implemented suppression ledger, a restore drill that re-applies suppression, and a verification report per disposition.

items.title: Delivery-time re-check of notification recipient authority and ownership generation
items.why_unresolved: Four contracts require that a notification be re-authorized at DELIVERY, not only when it is created: the guardian authority matrix ('background jobs, exports, files and notifications re-check authorization before execution/delivery'), the role-grantability matrix (revocation must not authorize a subsequent notification), the Saga recovery contract (a stale queued notification must not be delivered after a transfer) and the API authorization contract, which names 'stale queued notification after transfer' as a threat. Batch 8 enforces the recipient rule at INSERT. The delivery-time half needs a notification worker, and no worker, queue or delivery path exists in this repository.
items.security_impact: HIGH when a delivery path is built, and zero until then: nothing delivers a notification, so nothing can deliver a stale one. The specific risk is a notification queued before a guardian's permission was revoked, or before a student's ownership moved to another Workspace, being delivered afterwards.
items.continue_conditions: The insert-time rule is implemented and tested (OPS-10..OPS-16), the transfer write barrier now covers the notification table so a frozen student's notification cannot even be created (OPS-24, OPS-45), and the test header plus workspace_operations_draft.sql state plainly that delivery-time re-authorization is NOT implemented and NOT claimed. It overlaps PS-8, which holds the same gap for revocation freshness generally.
items.decision_owner: Product Owner with Platform Security; implementation belongs to the notification phase
options: A. The worker re-evaluates recipient authority, student lifecycle and current ownership generation inside the delivery transaction, and drops or quarantines anything that no longer passes.
B. Notifications carry the ownership generation they were created at, and delivery refuses on a generation mismatch.
C. Queue invalidation on revocation and on transfer: the event that revokes also purges or marks the affected queued notifications.
D. Short queue lifetime plus re-generation, so a stale notification expires rather than being re-checked.
items.rationale: (A) is what the contracts actually require, and this project's consistent lesson is that a check performed only at creation binds only the creator. (B) makes the transfer case cheap and deterministic and matches the generation fencing already used by the inbox projection, which is why recording the generation on the notification row is worth doing when the worker is built. (C) is a useful optimization but, on its own, is a cache invalidation problem and fails open if an invalidation is missed. (D) narrows the window without closing it.

evidence.implemented: insert-time recipient isolation and payload hygiene: docs/phase2/workspace/workspace_operations_draft.sql section 2
evidence.not_implemented: no notification worker, queue or delivery path exists in this repository

items.code_resolution_note: Delivery-time re-authorization is ordinary implementation in the notification phase; no decision blocks it beyond PS-8.
items.closure_evidence: A notification worker that re-checks authority and ownership generation in the delivery transaction, with tests for revocation and transfer between queueing and delivery.

items.title: Contact-shaped test fixtures remain in Git history
items.why_unresolved: The history content scan added on 2026-11-18 found 110 contact-shaped strings in old blobs and nothing else: six repeated-digit Iranian-mobile-shaped fixtures from the 2026-10-27..31 constraint tests and two test-run logs that echoed them, plus the two Batch 8 OPS-17/OPS-18 fixtures that failed CI. None was taken from data. They cannot be called unassigned numbers: the 0912-0917 prefixes are allocated, so a repeated-digit body may belong to a real subscriber. One of the Batch 8 values is in the North American fictional range (555-01xx) and is not a subscriber number. Removing any of them from history requires rewriting history and force-pushing, which is prohibited on this branch.
items.security_impact: LOW. They are not credentials, so nothing needs rotating or revoking. The residual risk is that a real subscriber's number appears in a test fixture in a repository history, against the spirit of D-014.
items.continue_conditions: Every finding is excepted individually in docs/phase2/tests/secret_scan_history_exceptions.json by (blob SHA, pattern, SHA-256 of the matched value), so a different finding in the same blob still fails CI; the working tree carries no such literal; the scanner never prints a detected number in full.
options: A. Accept the residual and keep the hashed exceptions.
B. Rewrite history to purge the blobs (filter-repo plus force-push), with every collaborator re-cloning; requires lifting the force-push prohibition.
C. Make the repository's visibility and access restrictions the compensating control and record that.
items.rationale: The values are not secrets and were not taken from people, so the benefit of a history rewrite is small and its cost (breaking every clone, invalidating every cited SHA in this project's evidence trail) is large. If any value is later shown to be a real person's number, B becomes the right answer.
items.code_resolution_note: Only a history rewrite removes them, and that is a decision, not code.
items.closure_evidence: A recorded Product Owner decision; if B, a post-rewrite scan with zero history exceptions.
